extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, attorneys seeking reinstatement, USPTO/OED staff, and legal counsel advising applicants on registration/examination/accommodation issues
extracted.subtask_description: Administrative decision interpreting USPTO rules for reinstatement to the patent practitioner register, access to registration examination materials, and reasonable testing accommodations under federal law. It evaluates petitions under 37 C.F.R. §§ 1.181 and 11.2(d), applying 37 C.F.R. § 11.7, 10.160(c), Section 504, and relevant case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director's statutory authority to require qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) the Director of the USPTO may require patent practitioners to show they are possessed of the necessary qualifications to render applicants valuable service, advice, and assistance in presenting or prosecuting applications before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory authority supports regulations and OED actions requiring an applicant seeking registration or reinstatement to demonstrate competency and qualifications before being placed on the register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement substantive requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.7(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: No individual will be registered unless established to the satisfaction of the OED Director that he or she: (i) possesses good moral character and reputation; (ii) possesses the legal, scientific, and technical qualifications necessary to render applicants valuable service; and (iii) is competent to advise and assist patent applicants in presentation and prosecution of their applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petitioner for reinstatement must affirmatively satisfy these elements; mere prior registration or prior practice does not automatically meet them after a long lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement after removal/inactive >5 years requires meeting registration requirements including examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Official policy (Official Gazette notice) and 37 C.F.R. § 10.160(c) permit the Director to require, as a condition of reinstatement, that an individual meet the requirements of 37 C.F.R. § 11.7, including taking and passing the registration examination if five or more years have elapsed since removal/inactive status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where more than five years have passed since removal/endorsement as inactive, the Office will generally require passing the registration exam before reinstatement is granted; a practitioner who resigned while disciplinary charges were pending typically gives up the right to practice absent satisfying reinstatement rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examinee's limited right to review failed examination materials (37 C.F.R. § 11.7(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Within sixty days of the mailing date of a notice of failure, an individual is entitled to inspect, but not copy, the questions and answers he or she incorrectly answered; the review is under supervision and no notes may be taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation affords supervised, on-site inspection within 60 days only; it does not permit copying, taking notes, or unlimited access. This limited inspection constitutes the administrative opportunity to examine the failed items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of exam questions and limitation on retaking identical prior exams
rubrics_metrics.description: The registration examination questions and answers are maintained in confidence (analogous to the MBE) to preserve exam integrity; allowing unlimited retakes of identical past exams or unlimited access to model answers would permit memorization and undermine substantive assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency policy and the Federal Register explanation justify limiting access to prior exams and refusing requests to re-administer identical prior forms; failed candidates may retake the registration examination an unlimited number of times, but the Office need not (and should not) permit reusing identical, previously administered question forms or unrestricted copying/review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency obligation to provide reasonable accommodation under Section 504
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act prohibits disability-based discrimination by federal agencies and requires the provision of reasonable accommodations to allow access to agency programs (29 U.S.C. § 794).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While agencies must provide reasonable accommodations, courts and administrative precedent make clear an examinee is not entitled to the accommodation of his choice; the agency must provide an effective accommodation. Case law cited includes Mennen v. U.S. Postal Service, Siuolo v. Dept. of the Navy, and Madison v. Dep't of Defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of medical evidence and nexus for requested accommodations
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner seeking particular testing accommodations must provide medical documentation showing the disability and a nexus between the disability and the specific accommodation requested (i.e., why the requested accommodation is necessary to address the disability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the medical documentation does not explain why a specific accommodation (e.g., two successive eight-hour sessions) is needed, the agency may lawfully provide an alternative effective accommodation. The petitioner bears the burden to demonstrate the necessity of non-standard accommodations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for assessing whether provided accommodations are effective
rubrics_metrics.description: An accommodation is sufficient if it is effective — it need not match the examinee's preferred accommodations; the examinee must show the provided accommodations were ineffective for his disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating effectiveness relies on the medical recommendations and the examinee's ability to complete the exam under the accommodation; absence of evidence the provided accommodation was ineffective supports denial of additional accommodations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural expectation to notify proctor of difficulties during examination
rubrics_metrics.description: An examinee who experiences problems during the exam (e.g., with reading the examination materials) must promptly notify the examination proctor at the time of the exam; failure to do so undermines later claims that accommodations provided were inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-exam complaints about performance without contemporaneous notice to the proctor weigh against finding the accommodation was inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of reasonable testing accommodations and OED's practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissible accommodations may include extended testing time, larger-font examination booklets and answer sheets, magnifiers, additional lighting, separate testing rooms, permission to bring assistive devices, desk lamps, and provision of large-print copies of reference materials (e.g., MPEP) under supervised conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision illustrates these as typical effective accommodations the Office may provide (e.g., two 4.5-hour sessions, 14-point font, magnifiers, separate room). Requests for additional or different accommodations must be medically justified and shown to be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on administrative review: claims outside the administrative record or frivolous
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations that are frivolous, unintelligible, or fall outside the purview of the proceeding or the record before the OED Director will not be further considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners must confine challenges to issues reflected in the administrative record and present intelligible, legally cognizable claims to obtain relief.
